$comment: THE TWELVE PUBLICATIONS METRICOOL ALREADY OWNS.
Read from the Metricool planner (brand 6744652, ALOP-AI) on 2026-08-19 and
frozen here because the ledger's whole job is to know what is already
spoken for BEFORE Buffer is allowed to write. An empty ledger believes
every reel/platform pair is free, which is exactly the state that produces
a double publish.
Four reels x three platforms. Two were already PUBLISHED when this was
read; the other ten were PENDING. Statuses are preserved as they were, not
normalised - `published` and `scheduled` are both active, so either way
Buffer is refused, but the operator reading the table should see which is
which.
NOTHING HERE IS EDITED INTO METRICOOL. This file is a record of that
planner's state, and importing it changes nothing on Metricool's side.
media is the Metricool CDN copy, which is what Metricool will actually
publish. Our own masters live in the Supabase `reels` bucket and are what
Buffer will use for FUTURE reels - the two are different URLs for the same
video on purpose, and the ledger records what each scheduler was handed.
publicUrl ON THE TIKTOK ROW HOLDS A HANDLE THAT NO LONGER EXISTS. The
account was renamed to @alop_ai on 2026-08-19 and @userma0e40g4sp now
404s as a profile. The URL is left exactly as it was read, because this
file is a record of the planner's state at readAt and not a live index.
Nothing reads this field: backfill() ingests reel_id, platform,
scheduler, scheduler_post_id, scheduled_at, status, media_url and
caption_hash, and publicUrl is dropped. Identity for anything that runs
is the Buffer channel id in EXPECTED_ACCOUNTS, never a handle - see
queue.mjs and the rename test in publish-buffer.test.js.

24 rows read. Or 1.

Without an index, a lookup reads rows one after another until it finds the match - a sequential scan.

An index is a sorted structure the database can descend, so it lands on the row instead of walking to it.

Run EXPLAIN on the query. If it says Seq Scan on a table you filter often, that is the fix.

12 scroll events. 1 handler call.

Every scroll, resize and keystroke fires far more often than your handler needs to run.

debounce restarts a timer on each event and only runs the callback once the events stop.

The whole trick is the clearTimeout: each call cancels the pending one.

8 rows. 9 queries. Every request.

One query fetches the list, then the loop fires another query per row to fetch what it references.

That is the N+1: it looks like clean code and it scales linearly in round trips.

Ask for the related rows in the first query instead and the whole loop collapses into one trip.

50 requests. 100 selects on the same table.

Your auth middleware reads the users row to check whether the account is suspended. It caches it. Then the next helper down the chain selects the same row again, microseconds later, because it has no idea the first one already has it.

Fifteen call sites were paying for that second read — every route with an :id in it.

The fix is not to thread a cached row through fifteen callers. It is one guard inside the function they all already share: check the cache before you select.

Comment CACHE and I'll send the fix.
